652.title: Peace be with you (John 20:19–23)
652.hook: behind locked doors he breathes on them: receive the Holy Spirit
652.howItsDone: In many churches the minister greets the congregation with 'peace be with you' or 'the Lord be with you', and Catholic and Orthodox Christians link this passage with the sacrament of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary turned at her name and said Rabboni. Your line was I have seen the lord. Who did you tell about something good you'd seen? Day six hundred fifty-two.

It's the evening of that same Sunday. Mary has told them. They've heard the tomb is empty. And where are they? In a room with the doors locked. John says they're afraid of the authorities who had Jesus arrested. The news has reached them, and they're still behind a bolted door, listening for footsteps on the stairs. Good news, it turns out, doesn't unlock a door by itself. And then, without a knock, he's standing among them.

His first words, in the King James Bible: "Peace be unto you." It's an everyday greeting, like the Hebrew shalom, the hello anyone might say coming through a door. But look at who's saying it, and to whom. These are the friends who ran, who hid, one of whom denied knowing him three times. He doesn't start with, where were you? He starts with peace. Then he shows them his hands and his side, the wounds still there. And John says: "Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord." He says it again, peace be unto you, and gives them a job: "as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you." Then the strangest gesture in the passage: "he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost." Readers have long heard an echo of Genesis here, where God breathes into the first human and he becomes a living soul; the old Greek translation of Genesis uses the same verb John does. If the echo is meant, this is a new creation, a new beginning, starting in a locked room. Then he speaks about forgiving sins: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven. Churches read that line in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see in it the authority given to the church to forgive sins in confession. Many Protestants hear it as the power given to every believer to proclaim forgiveness in Jesus's name. In every reading, forgiveness sits at the center of that first evening.
screen: `AS THE FATHER SENT ME, I SEND YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe out peace. Settle, and breathe. Notice your own locked room today: the worry you keep the door bolted on. Breathe in slowly. As you breathe out, let the word peace go out with your breath, toward that worry. Then toward someone who's let you down. Then toward someone you've let down. Peace, on the out-breath, each time. If you pray, you can receive his words as spoken to you: peace be unto you. If you don't, simply let your breath carry goodwill. The bell holds the time.
Peace be with you. The risen Jesus's first words to friends who had run away, spoken through a locked door.
Your line: peace be with you. Today, start one hard conversation with peace instead of with where were you. Day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: That you may believe (John 20:24–31)
653.hook: Thomas says my Lord and my God, and John tells us why he wrote
653.howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Thomas on the Sunday after Easter, and Christians in India's Saint Thomas tradition honor him as the apostle who brought them the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a locked room, and his first words. Your line was peace be with you. Did you start a hard conversation with peace? Day six hundred fifty-three.

One of the twelve wasn't in the room that Sunday. Thomas, called the twin. When the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he gives a no that people still quote. Unless I see the nail prints, and put my finger in them, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. Later readers gave him a nickname: Doubting Thomas. The Gospel never calls him that. And a week later, he's the one who says the words this Gospel opened with, to Jesus's face.
screen: `UNLESS I SEE, I WILL NOT BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Eight days later they're in the room again, doors shut, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus stands among them, says peace be with you, and turns straight to Thomas. He offers exactly what Thomas asked for: reach here your finger, behold my hands, reach your hand into my side. And then: be not faithless, but believing. Here's what's striking. The text never says Thomas touched him. Painters, like Caravaggio, show his finger in the wound. John doesn't. What John records is the answer. In the King James Bible: "And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God." Remember how this Gospel began: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. Now, near the end, the disciple who asked for proof says it to his face. The book has come full circle. Then Jesus: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." That line isn't about Thomas. It's about everyone after him, everyone reading. And then John stops and tells you why he wrote: "many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book: But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name." Not to win an argument. That you might have life. It reads like an ending, and some readers think it once was one, with chapter twenty-one added after. Tradition says Thomas later carried the news east, as far as India, where the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to him.
screen: `MY LORD AND MY GOD: FULL CIRCLE.`
`WHY JOHN WROTE: THAT YOU MIGHT HAVE LIFE.`
then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HAVE NOT SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read verse thirty-one. Settle, and breathe. Let the words come slowly: these are written, that ye might believe, and that believing ye might have life through his name. Say the last part again: that ye might have life. Notice where you're hungry for life right now: more energy, more meaning, more joy. Let the verse sit beside that hunger. If you pray, you can ask for that life. If you have doubts, Thomas's honesty is welcome here too. The bell holds the time.
That you may believe. John's own reason for writing: these signs are written so you might believe, and believing, have life.
Your line: that you might have life. Today, do one thing that makes you more alive, and if you have an honest question, say it out loud, like Thomas. Day six hundred fifty-three.

654.title: Come and dine (John 21:1–14)
654.hook: a hundred and fifty-three fish, and breakfast on the shore
654.howItsDone: Many churches read this story in the Easter season, and some Christians remember it at shared meals and church breakfasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas said my Lord and my God, and John told us why he wrote. Your line was that you might have life. What made you more alive? Day six hundred fifty-four.

After everything in Jerusalem, what do the disciples do? They go back to Galilee, and Peter says, in the King James Bible, "I go a fishing." Six others say, we'll come too. Maybe that's what hands do after an upheaval: they go back to what they know. They fish all night on the Sea of Tiberias, and catch nothing. At dawn there's a man standing on the shore. They don't recognize him. And he calls out to them the way you'd call to a group of boys: children, have you any meat? Got anything to eat? No, they say.
screen: `A STRANGER ON THE SHORE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Cast the net on the right side of the ship, he says, and ye shall find. They do, and suddenly they can't haul it in for the weight of fish. And the beloved disciple, who outran Peter to the tomb, is the first to understand again. He says: "It is the Lord." Peter, being Peter, grabs his coat and jumps into the sea, and the others row the boat in, dragging the net. And when they get to land: "they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread." A fire of coals. We've stood by one before, in the courtyard, where Peter warmed his hands and said, I am not. Hold onto that for tomorrow. Then the number. Peter drags the net ashore, "full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken." Why would anyone count? Maybe someone simply did, the way fishermen tally a catch. Ancient readers went further. Jerome said ancient naturalists counted a hundred fifty-three kinds of fish, so the net held every kind of person. Augustine noticed that a hundred fifty-three is the sum of every number from one to seventeen. The text doesn't explain. Some readers see the unbroken net as a picture of a church big enough for everyone. And then the line in today's carry: "Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine." Breakfast. He's already cooked. The risen Lord, on a beach, making breakfast for tired fishermen.
screen: `IT IS THE LORD, AND PETER JUMPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make breakfast for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's had a long night, literally or not. A roommate, a partner, a coworker on the early shift, a parent with a new baby. Picture making them something simple. Toast. Coffee. Eggs. Fruit cut up on a plate. Picture handing it to them without asking for anything back. If you pray, you can give thanks for whoever has fed you. If you don't, simply remember the last time someone cooked for you. The bell holds the time.
Come and dine. The risen Jesus's invitation on the shore, with fish on a charcoal fire, to friends who fished all night and caught nothing.
Your line: come and dine. Tomorrow morning, or today, make breakfast or bring coffee for someone who's tired, and don't make a big deal of it. Day six hundred fifty-four.

655.title: Feed my sheep (John 21:15–19)
655.hook: three times: do you love me? feed my lambs
655.tomorrow: John close: all the books in the world
655.howItsDone: Many churches read this passage at ordinations of priests and pastors, and Catholics read it on feasts of Saint Peter, linking it with the ministry of the pope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hundred fifty-three fish and breakfast on the beach. Your line was come and dine. Who did you feed? Day six hundred fifty-five.

Breakfast is over. The fish bones are on the coals. Peter is still sitting by the charcoal fire from yesterday's story, the one that echoes the courtyard fire where he said, I am not. Three times. John never tells us that anyone has spoken of it since. And now Jesus turns to him, in front of the others, and asks him a question. Then asks again. Then a third time. Everyone at that fire can count.

In the King James Bible: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs." Notice the name. Not Peter, the rock. Simon, son of Jonas: the name he had before any of this began. Then a second time: lovest thou me? Yes, Lord. Tend my sheep. Then a third. And John says: "Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me?" He knows what three means. But this time Peter doesn't argue or boast like he did at the supper. He just says: "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee." You know everything. Including that night. And the answer each time is not a lecture. It's a job. Feed my sheep. Three denials, three questions, three commissions. The wound is opened, gently, so it can heal. You may hear sermons about the Greek words for love here. Jesus asks twice with agapao and once with phileo, and Peter answers each time with phileo. Some readers see a deep difference. Many scholars point out that John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere, so the shift may be style more than meaning. Either way, the heart of the scene is the same. Churches read this commission differently. Catholics see here Peter's special role as chief shepherd of the whole church, which they believe passes to the popes. Orthodox and Protestant Christians honor Peter's restoration, and many hear in it a calling for every pastor and every believer. Then Jesus tells Peter that one day he'll be led where he doesn't want to go, and says the two words that have run through the whole story: follow me.
screen: `SIMON, SON OF JONAS: THE OLD NAME.`
`THE THIRD TIME, AND PETER IS GRIEVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for one person today. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone in your life who's like a sheep without much tending right now. Someone overlooked, tired, new, lonely, or just a little lost. Picture their face. What would feeding them look like? A meal. A call. Help with a task. An hour of your attention. Choose one concrete thing. If you pray, you can hear the question asked of you, gently, and answer it with that one thing. If you don't, simply commit to it. The bell holds the time.
Feed my sheep. Three questions by a charcoal fire, three answers, and each time a job: look after the ones I love.
Your line: feed my sheep. Today, do the one concrete thing you chose for the person you pictured, before the evening. Day six hundred fifty-five.

656.title: John close: all the books in the world (John 21:20–25)
656.hook: if everything were written down, the world couldn't contain the books
656.carry: the world could not contain it
656.howItsDone: In many churches, readings from John fill the weeks of Lent and Easter, and some Christians read the Gospel straight through as a whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three questions by a charcoal fire. Your line was feed my sheep. Who did you look after? Day six hundred fifty-six, and the last day in John.

Peter has just been forgiven, given a job, and told follow me. And what's the very first thing he does? He turns around, sees the beloved disciple walking behind them, and asks: "Lord, and what shall this man do?" What about him? It's a very human question: barely handed a calling of his own, Peter is already checking someone else's. Is his harder? Easier? Does he get the better ending? Jesus's answer is short, and it's the last thing he says in John's Gospel.

"If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me." What is that to you? Your path is yours. And then John clears up a rumor. People had started saying this disciple would never die. John says, Jesus never said that. He only said, if I want him to stay, what is that to you? It seems the community needed that set straight, perhaps after the beloved disciple had died. Then a signature, of sorts: "This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true." We. Other voices, standing behind the witness, vouching for him. And then the last verse of the Gospel, with a wink: "there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written." A Gospel that began with the Word, before time, ends with books, more books than the world could hold. The Greek word is biblia, little scrolls, the word that gave us Bible. We've spent sixty-five days in this Gospel. Here's what we carried. The Word and the Lamb. Come and see, under the fig tree, water into wine. Born from above, for God so loved. A Samaritan woman at a well. Bread of life, light of the world, the truth will set you free. The good shepherd, Lazarus, Jesus wept. A grain of wheat, feet washed, a new commandment, many rooms, the vine. Then the garden, the fire, ecce homo, it is finished. And Rabboni, peace be with you, my Lord and my God, come and dine, feed my sheep. Tomorrow we open a letter, written by Paul, from prison, full of joy.
screen: `WHAT IS THAT TO THEE? FOLLOW THOU ME.`
`BIBLIA: MORE BOOKS THAN THE WORLD COULD HOLD.`
then, large: `THE WORLD ITSELF COULD NOT CONTAIN THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line of your own witness. Settle, and breathe. Think back over these weeks in John. Which scene stayed with you? A word, a line, a face. Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one that actually stuck. Now shape one sentence about it, in your own words. Something you've seen, or wondered, or felt. If you pray, it can be a line of thanks. If you're learning, it can be a question. After the sit, write it down somewhere you'll find it again. The bell holds the time.
John close. The end of the fourth Gospel: follow thou me, a witness vouched for, and more books than the world could hold.
Your line: the world could not contain it. Today, write your one line of witness down, and if someone asks what you're reading, tell them. Day six hundred fifty-six, and John is complete.

657.title: I thank my God (Philippians 1:1–11)
657.hook: Paul, in prison, thanks God every time he remembers them
657.howItsDone: Many Christians begin their prayers with thanksgiving for particular people, as Paul does, and some write Philippians 1:6 in cards for people starting something new or going through a slow season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day in John, and more books than the world could contain. Your line was the world could not contain it. What line of witness did you write? Day six hundred fifty-seven, and a new block begins.

Over the next weeks we read three short letters, one after another: Philippians, James, and the first letter of John. Joy, faith and love. And we start with a thank-you note written by a prisoner. Paul is in chains. Scholars debate where: Rome, Ephesus, maybe Caesarea. He doesn't know if he'll be released or executed. And he writes to a small church in a Roman colony in northern Greece, a church that's been sending him money and help. A letter from prison might open with complaint, or fear, or a request. Instead, the first thing Paul says is thank you.

In the King James Bible: "I thank my God upon every remembrance of you." Every remembrance. Every time they come to mind, he gives thanks. Who are they? In the book of Acts, Paul comes to Philippi after a vision of a man of Macedonia asking for help. Lydia, a businesswoman who sold purple cloth, is baptized there with her household. Then a jailer, after an earthquake shakes open the prison doors one night. A merchant and a prison guard, among the church's first members. And they've stuck with Paul ever since. He thanks them "For your fellowship in the gospel from the first day until now." Fellowship is the Greek koinonia: partnership, sharing, a common life. Here it's practical. They shared his work, and later in the letter he thanks them for sending money more than once, when no other church did. Then the confidence: "he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ." Paul doesn't say you'll finish what you started. He says God will finish what he started in you. Some readers hold onto that line in slow seasons, when they feel unfinished. And then he prays for them: "that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment." Not just more love. Love that sees clearly, love with good judgment. One word keeps surfacing through this short letter, again and again: joy. Rejoice. From a prison cell. That's the thread we'll follow for the next few weeks.
screen: `EVERY TIME THEY COME TO MIND: THANKS.`
`LYDIA AND A JAILER: THE FIRST CHURCH.`
then, large: `I THANK MY GOD UPON EVERY REMEMBRANCE OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone you remember. Settle, and breathe. Let a face come to mind, someone who has been a partner to you in something good. A teacher, an old friend, a coworker who covered for you, someone who believed in you early. Stay with that memory. What did they actually do? Let gratitude rise without rushing it. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name, the way Paul did. If you don't, simply hold them in thanks for these minutes. The bell holds the time.
I thank my God. Paul's first words to the Philippians, from prison: thanks for them every time they come to mind.
Your line: every remembrance. Today, send the person you remembered a short note: I thought of you, and I'm grateful. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

658.title: To live is Christ (Philippians 1:12–26)
658.hook: his chains have spread the news; to live is Christ, to die is gain
658.howItsDone: Some Christians facing illness, prison or danger turn to Philippians 1:21, and it is sometimes read at Christian funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prisoner opened his letter with I thank my God. Your line was every remembrance. Did you send your note of thanks? Day six hundred fifty-eight.

Chains, and a guard who never leaves. In this letter Paul calls them his bonds, and he is plainly under guard. Every visitor is seen. Every letter he dictates, someone overhears. Every prayer, too. Plenty of people would call that the end of their work. Paul looks at the same situation and sees an audience. The friends at Philippi are worried about him. So he writes to tell them how it's actually going.

In the King James Bible: "the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel." The prison has helped, not hurt. "So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace." Palace here is the praetorium, the Roman guard or the governor's headquarters. The whole guard knows why he's chained. And other believers, seeing him unafraid, have grown bolder. Then he admits something surprising. Some people are preaching about Christ out of rivalry, hoping to make his chains hurt more. His response? "What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice." He doesn't need to be the hero of the story. Then the line in today's title and carry: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." He's thinking out loud about his own trial. If he lives, he keeps working, which for him is Christ. If he dies, he's with Christ, which he calls far better. "I am in a strait betwixt two": hemmed in on both sides, pulled two ways. And then he chooses, as far as it's his choice: to stay is more needful for you. He'll live for them. The passage is honest. It doesn't pretend death is nothing. It says that a life wrapped around something larger is a life that even prison can't shrink. Here's the week we've walked: peace in a locked room, Thomas, breakfast, feed my sheep, the end of John, a thank-you from prison, and now a man who turns chains into a pulpit.
screen: then, large: `FOR TO ME TO LIVE IS CHRIST, AND TO DIE IS GAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a good in your constraint. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing that's hemming you in right now. A job you can't leave yet. An illness. Caring for a parent. Money. A season of waiting. Don't pretend it's good. Just look at it honestly. Then ask: who is around me inside this, that I wouldn't meet otherwise? What can I do here that I couldn't do anywhere else? Find one thing, even small. If you pray, you can offer the constraint to God. The bell holds the time.
To live is Christ. Paul's line from prison: living means serving Christ, and dying means being with him, so even chains can't shrink his life.
Your line: to live is christ. Today, inside the constraint you named, do the one good thing you found there. Day six hundred fifty-eight, and another week on the path.

myth: Paul says his imprisonment has helped spread the gospel
"the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel."
Paul is angry at people who preach out of rivalry
"whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice."
in this passage Paul says death is nothing to him
he weighs it honestly, calls being with Christ far better, and chooses to stay for their sake.

fork.setup: you're in chains. you hear that some people are preaching just to make your situation worse. how do you respond?
options: write a letter denouncing them.
rejoice that Christ is preached either way.
stop writing until you're free.
fork.reveal: "What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice."

original.note: Greek: to live, Christ. Paul's line is even shorter in Greek than in English.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about not fearing death.
what it means: a prisoner weighing life and death honestly, and choosing to live for his friends.
what a scholar hears: praetorium (1:13), which some take as the guard in Rome and others as a governor's headquarters elsewhere, part of the debate about where Paul was held.
